summary: Documents the charter of the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG), the body that manages the day-to-day technical work of the IETF. It records how the IESG was understood to operate when it was written. It was later updated by RFC 3932, RFC 5742 and RFC 8717.

eli5.summary: A club has a small group of leaders who keep things running. This note writes down what that group is for and how it works, so everyone knows.

subtitle: A written description of what the IESG does to run the IETF and keep its output good.

tldr.problem: The Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) had been doing its job for years, but no single document described its tasks as they were then understood.
tldr.mechanism: The memo documents existing practice: who sits on the IESG, how it decides, and its roles in working groups, document review, area management and appeals.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational record of practice in spring 2003, not an IETF consensus statement, and it has since been updated by RFC 3932, RFC 5742 and RFC 8717.

facts.label: Ex-officio members
facts.value: IAB Chair and IETF Executive Director

facts.label: IAB-style voting rule
facts.value: Two thirds concur, no more than two dissents

today: RFC 3710 is an Informational RFC that has been updated by RFC 3932, RFC 5742 and RFC 8717. It records IESG practice as understood in 2003 and says it is not IETF consensus on what the IESG should do.

sections.title: The Role of the IESG
sections.content:
The IESG is the group responsible for the direct operation of the IETF and for ensuring the quality of work produced by the IETF. It charters and terminates working groups, selects their chairs, monitors their progress and coordinates efforts between them.

It also performs technical review and approval of working group documents and candidates for the IETF standards track, and reviews other candidates for publication in the RFC series. It administers IETF logistics, including the Internet-Draft series and the IETF meeting event.

The role has been largely constant since 1993. The memo says it was written as a documentation of existing practice while the IETF structure was being reevaluated, so it does not claim to be IETF consensus on what the IESG should do. It describes tasks, not detailed procedures.
sections.eli5: The IESG is like the group of team captains for a big club. They start and stop clubs-within-the-club, check that the work is good, and plan the meetings.

sections.title: Who Sits on the IESG
sections.content:
The members are the IETF Chair (who also acts as the General Area Director when that area is active) and the Area Directors (ADs) for the IETF areas. The IAB Chair and the IETF Executive Director are ex-officio members. The IETF Chair and the ADs are selected by the IETF NomCom under the procedures of BCP 10.

The IESG also has liaisons who may attend all IESG meetings. When the memo was written they represented the RFC Editor, the IANA and the IAB. Members of the IETF Secretariat are on the mailing list and attend as needed for support.

Only the IETF Chair and the Area Directors make IESG decisions, although all IESG members can take part in the discussions.
sections.eli5: Some people are full voting members, and some are helpers who can listen and talk but do not get a vote.

sections.title: Decisions, Openness and Confidentiality
sections.content:
The IESG attempts to reach all decisions unanimously. If it cannot, the chair may conduct informal polls. There is no general voting rule, but if one were needed the memo says it is likely to be the IAB rule: at least two thirds concur and no more than two dissent. Only the IETF Chair and ADs count when judging consensus.

Some decisions use other procedures: assertions of IETF consensus (which need due notice and a chance for community feedback), IESG actions within its authority, AD actions with the advice and consent of the IESG, and independent AD actions.

The IESG publishes a record of its decisions and holds an open meeting at every IETF meeting. It also has private discussions, whose records need not be made public, because that allows a frank exchange of views. Decisions and their justification are a matter of public record. Personnel, legal and financial matters may be kept confidential.
sections.eli5: The leaders try to agree on everything. They talk some things over in private so people can speak honestly, but what they decide, and why, is shared with everyone.

sections.title: Working Groups, Areas and Appeals
sections.content:
The IESG manages the working group (WG) process. Most of that is delegated to the responsible Area Director. A WG chair manages the group from the inside (people, drafts, meetings, lists). An AD manages it from the outside (charters, chairs, cross-group relationships). The AD picks and, when necessary, replaces WG chairs, and the final decision to charter a WG belongs to the IESG. Terminating a WG is a decision of the responsible AD and is announced with a reason.

The IESG defines the area structure and can add, merge, redefine or close areas, in consultation with the community. It can only add new members through the NomCom process. Each area has one or two ADs, who may be advised by directorates.

Most decisions by a WG chair can be appealed to the AD, decisions by an individual AD to the IESG, and decisions of the IESG to the IAB. The IAB chair and the IAB liaison recuse themselves from discussion of appeals to the IESG.
sections.eli5: Each small group has its own leader for day-to-day things. A bigger leader watches over several groups. If you disagree with a decision, you can ask the next leader up to look again.

sections.title: Reviewing Documents
sections.content:
The IESG is expected to make sure documents are good enough to be released as RFCs, describe their subject well, and have no outstanding engineering issues. How deep the review goes depends on the intended status and perceived importance of the document.

For standards-track documents that do not come from a working group, the IESG decides whether the specification is appropriate for the standards track, whether it needs review by an existing WG, and whether its quality is adequate. No document can be published on the standards track without IESG approval. The IESG may also decide that a document should be published as Experimental, Informational or a BCP instead.

Informational and Experimental documents normally go to the RFC Editor, and the IESG reviews them for conflicts with the IETF standards process. It may recommend publishing as is, review by a WG, publishing with an IESG note, or not publishing. For every document the IESG assigns a specific AD to shepherd it.
sections.eli5: Before a note goes into the official book, the leaders read it. They can say yes, ask for fixes, or add a warning label.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says the security of the Internet depends on standards giving proper thought to security. Apart from that, it finds no security considerations relevant to the memo itself.
sections.eli5: This note is about how a group is run, so it has nothing special to say about keeping computers safe.
